paras: The burning of Randall McCoy's house was a night attack on McCoy's home on the Blackberry Fork of Pond Creek, Pike County, Kentucky, on or about January 1, 1888, in which attackers fired the house and shot the family as they came out. McCoy's daughter and a son were killed and his wife badly wounded; McCoy escaped. Papers across the country blamed the Hatfields of Logan County, West Virginia, as the latest act of the Hatfield-McCoy feud, though a Logan County state senator denied they took part.

According to a Catlettsburg dispatch, the feud dated from an election about five years earlier at which McCoy brothers fatally stabbed Ellison Hatfield, after which Hatfield relatives tied three McCoy boys to a pawpaw bush and shot them. A Pikeville correspondent wrote that about twenty-three men had been indicted for those killings and that in October 1887 Kentucky's governor offered rewards for four of them, among them Cap and Johnson Hatfield.

State Senator John B. Floyd of Logan County told a Charleston correspondent that a Pike County lawyer, P. A. Cline, had revived the indictments for money and that Frank Phillips and John Kite had drawn Randall McCoy into hunting the Hatfields.

The Pikeville correspondent, Floyd and the Richmond Daily Times all placed the attack on the night of January 1. In the Daily Times version, about a dozen Hatfields called on McCoy to surrender before firing his log cabin. The Catlettsburg dispatch said McCoy's eldest daughter, printed as Alafara or Alfara, was shot dead from concealment when she opened the door, and his son Calvin after her. McCoy's wife was shot through the head as she fled the burning building and was not expected to live.
McCoy escaped with his shotgun and, according to the dispatch, killed a member of the gang named Chambers and reportedly wounded Cap Hatfield.

By January 15 Mrs. McCoy had been brought to Pikeville and was recovering. Soon after, a Pike County posse led by Frank Phillips crossed into West Virginia, killed James Vance, and brought several indicted men back to the Pike County jail. No arrest or indictment for the burning itself appears in the coverage.

On February 1 an agent of West Virginia's Governor Wilson reported that Pike County men had "kidnapped" nine West Virginians and that the Hatfields were law-abiding. In September a Pikeville dispatch reported all the prisoners in "the Hatfield trial" acquitted, without naming the charges.

The story spread through a Catlettsburg special to the Cincinnati Enquirer, printed on January 9 by the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and on January 13 by the Hazel Green Herald. It called the burning "one of the most wanton and diabolical cases of arson and murder ever committed in the State of Kentucky" and the attackers "fiends." The Rock Island Daily Argus headed it "Characteristic Incident of Life in Watterson's State."

A Baltimore American special from Parkersburg, placing the house in Logan County, ran as "The Usual End of a Feud" in the Shepherdstown Register and "Frightful Deed" in the Shenandoah Herald. A January 20 Charleston special recalled McCoy's wife, son and daughter driven "like sheep into the shambles."

West Virginia papers soon carried the Hatfields' side; the Wheeling Register headed Floyd's interview "Hatfields Declared Innocent" and printed his claim that affidavits placed each Hatfield elsewhere. The Point Pleasant Weekly Register, reprinting the Wayne News, allowed that the Hatfields or their friends "may have burned" the house but called the Kentucky posse "bloodhounds" who "put law to shame." No paper named anyone's race.

The Catlettsburg dispatch and a Charleston special put the house in Kentucky, while the Parkersburg special placed it in Logan County, West Virginia. The Pikeville correspondent, writing from the town where Mrs. McCoy was being treated, supports Kentucky. Reports also differ on whether the son died at once, where the mother was hit, and the date ("Wednesday night" in the Shepherdstown Register).

The dispatch's report that McCoy killed Chambers conflicts with the Pikeville correspondent, who knew of no dead man but Vance. Responsibility was also disputed: the dispatch laid the crime "at the door of the notorious Hatfields," the Parkersburg special called them only suspected, and Floyd said they "knew nothing" of it.

reader.title: Burning of Randall McCoy's house
bases: A night raid in a family feud in which attackers burned a house and shot the occupants as they came out (A1, A11, A17); no crime accusation against the victims and no race is stated, so it fits none of the lynching or racial-violence categories cleanly.

The Catlettsburg dispatch (A1, A2), the separate Parkersburg special (A5, A14), a Pikeville letter (A11) and the Hatfields' own defender (A9) all agree that McCoy's house was burned and his son and daughter shot, though who did it is contested (A9, A10).

accounts.label: Senator John B. Floyd (Hatfield side)
